**In Praise of Lingering**

We live in an age that worships speed. Productivity is measured in tasks completed, messages answered, miles traveled. The fastest seems to win. But I want to make a case for the opposite: slowness, lingering, attention without obvious payoff. Not as a lifestyle trend or productivity hack, but as a quiet rebellion against the idea that every moment must be optimized.

I first noticed this when I began taking walks without my phone. At first, my hand kept drifting to my pocket. Without a podcast, my thoughts felt too loud. But after a few days, I started hearing the layered sounds of my neighborhood: crows, a distant lawnmower, a shovel scraping concrete. I noticed late-afternoon light turning brick walls into gold. I felt bored—and discovered that boredom was not emptiness but spaciousness.

We have lost the ability to linger. Public spaces are designed for movement. Benches are removed to discourage loitering. Coffee shops limit Wi-Fi. The message is clear: keep moving, keep consuming. Yet some of the most important human experiences happen when we stay put. Friendship deepens in the unplanned hour after a meal. Ideas emerge from a walk with no destination. Grief and joy need time to be felt.

The pressure to be productive has seeped into leisure. We turn hobbies into side hustles. We read books to say we read them. Even rest becomes performance—the styled nap, the documented retreat. We forget that the most restorative moments are often unremarkable: sitting on a step, watching rain, letting the mind wander.

Attention is not a switch. It is a muscle. And it grows in the moments we consider wasted. When we stare out a window, our brain enters the default mode network, linked to memory, reflection, and creativity. Daydreaming is not nothing. It is soil for new thoughts.

Yet our culture treats daydreaming as a flaw, especially in children. We fill every hour with structured activities. We forget that Archimedes had his insight in the bath, Newton under an apple tree, Einstein imagining riding a beam of light. None happened in a meeting. They happened in unstructured time.

Technology, for all its gifts, is engineered to capture attention. Infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications—these are not accidents. They are designed to keep us from lingering. Each interruption fragments our attention, making it harder to regain focus. Studies suggest that after a distraction, it can take over twenty minutes to return to deep concentration. We are not simply distracted; we are being trained to expect interruption. Choosing slowness often means choosing friction: putting the phone in another room, disabling notifications, using a paper map. These small acts of defiance create the conditions for attention to flourish.

I am not arguing for laziness. Slowness is a choice to give something full attention, even if it is not urgent. It is cooking from scratch, writing a letter, reading a poem twice. These acts are not conventionally productive, but they produce a richer texture of life.

The pressure to optimize also flattens our emotions. We want quick fixes for sadness, anxiety, boredom. But emotions have their own pace. Grief cannot be rushed. Love does not follow a timeline. Slowness lets us feel without immediately escaping.

In many spiritual traditions, slowness is prayer. Benedictine monks practice *statio*—the art of stopping. Before moving to the next task, they pause. This prevents life from becoming a blur. We could borrow this: pause before checking a phone, opening a door, responding. Micro-pauses create space for choice rather than reflex.

Slowness is also connected to justice. Systems that exploit us rely on speed—making us feel there is no time to question or rest. The demand to be always available is a demand to be compliant. Reclaiming time is reclaiming power. Refusing to be hurried is a quiet political act.

Of course, not everyone can choose slowness. Many work multiple jobs or survive in conditions where time is not their own. But small acts remain: a breath before the next shift, no email during a meal, a walk around the block. They remind us we are human, not machines.

Even if you cannot change your schedule, you can change your relationship to time. Waiting in line can be a chance to breathe rather than scroll. A commute can be a time to look out the window. Chores can be done with attention rather than resentment. The point is not to add more slow activities to an already full life, but to bring slowness into the activities already there. This shift is subtle, but it changes everything. It turns time from an enemy into an ally.

The Japanese word *yutori* means spaciousness. A life with yutori has margins—time for rest, play, unexpected encounters. Without margins, any small disruption becomes crisis. With margins, we can absorb shock and still care for others.

I think of my grandmother, who never seemed to hurry. She moved slowly through her kitchen, peeling apples, humming. As a child, I found this maddening. Now I understand: she was not slow because she couldn't be fast. She was slow because she had decided what mattered—the taste of apples, the warmth of the kitchen, the presence of a grandchild. She was lingering.

We need more lingerers. More people who will sit on a bench and watch. More people who ask a question and actually wait for the answer. The lost art of lingering is not lost because we forgot how. It is lost because we stopped believing it was worth doing. But it is still there, waiting for us to slow down enough to find it.

Slowness is not about getting less done. It is about doing less in a way that means more. It is about reclaiming the texture of our days, the taste of our food, the sound of our own thoughts. We are not here merely to be productive. We are here to be present. And presence requires time—not measured time, but lived time. So today, walk somewhere without purpose. Sit for ten minutes without a screen. Let a conversation extend beyond its natural ending. Linger. You might be surprised at what you find.

Title: The Lost Art of Lingering

We live in an age that worships speed. We measure productivity in tasks completed, messages answered, miles traveled. The person who moves fastest seems to win. But I want to make a case for the opposite: for slowness, for lingering, for the kind of attention that has no obvious payoff. Not as a lifestyle trend or a productivity hack disguised as mindfulness, but as a quiet rebellion against the idea that every moment must be optimized.

I first noticed this when I began taking walks without my phone. At first, the absence felt like a missing limb. My hand kept drifting to my pocket, expecting the familiar rectangle. Without a podcast or playlist, my thoughts seemed too loud, too unstructured. But after a few days, something shifted. I started hearing the layered sounds of my neighborhood: the argumentative crows, the distant hum of a lawnmower, the scrape of a shovel against concrete. I noticed the way late-afternoon light turned ordinary brick walls into tapestries of gold and shadow. I noticed that I was, for the first time in months, actually bored—and that boredom was not an emptiness to be filled but a spaciousness to be explored.

We have largely lost the ability to linger. Public spaces are designed for movement, not staying. Benches are removed to discourage loitering. Coffee shops limit Wi-Fi time. Even parks are filled with fitness stations and scheduled activities. The message is clear: keep moving, keep consuming, keep producing. Yet some of the most important human experiences happen when we stay put. Friendship deepens in the unplanned hour after a meal. Ideas emerge from the long walk with no destination. Grief and joy both require time to be felt, not just acknowledged.

The pressure to be constantly productive has seeped into our leisure. We talk about "quality time" as if it must be curated and photographed. We turn hobbies into side hustles. We read books with the goal of saying we read them, not for the slow pleasure of sentences. Even rest becomes a performance: the perfectly styled nap, the wellness retreat that must be documented. In all this, we forget that the most restorative moments are often the most unremarkable. Sitting on a step. Watching rain. Listening to a friend ramble. Letting the mind wander without a destination.

There is a particular kind of attention that only slowness allows. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, "Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it." But attention is not a switch we flip. It is more like a muscle that grows with use. And it is often built in the moments we consider wasted. When we stare out a window, our brain enters a mode called the default mode network, which is associated with memory consolidation, self-reflection, and creativity. In other words, daydreaming is not nothing. It is the soil in which new thoughts grow.

Yet our culture treats daydreaming as a flaw, especially in children. We medicate inattention and fill every hour with structured activities. We forget that some of history's greatest discoveries came from minds that wandered: Archimedes in the bath, Newton under the apple tree, Einstein imagining himself riding a beam of light. None of these moments happened in a meeting. They happened in the spaciousness of unstructured time.

I am not arguing for laziness. There is a difference between slowness and idleness without intention. Slowness is a choice to give something our full attention, even if it is not urgent. It is the decision to cook a meal from scratch rather than reheating something, not because it is more efficient, but because the process itself has meaning. It is writing a letter by hand, walking to a friend's house instead of driving, reading a poem twice. These acts are not productive in the conventional sense, but they produce something else: a texture of life that is richer and more connected.

The pressure to optimize also flattens our emotional lives. We want quick fixes for sadness, anxiety, boredom. We want to feel better now, preferably with minimal discomfort. But emotions have their own pace. Grief cannot be rushed. Recovery cannot be scheduled. Love does not follow a timeline. When we try to speed up these processes, we end up numb or fragmented. Slowness, in contrast, allows us to feel the full range of our experience without immediately trying to escape it.

In many spiritual traditions, slowness is a form of prayer. The Benedictine monks have a practice called statio, the art of stopping. Before moving from one activity to the next, they pause. They allow a moment of silence to settle between tasks. This small habit prevents life from becoming a blur. It acknowledges that each moment has its own weight and worth. We could borrow this practice in secular form: before checking our phone, pause. Before opening a door, pause. Before responding to a difficult question, pause. These micro-pauses create space for choice rather than reflex.

I have also come to believe that slowness is deeply connected to justice. The systems that exploit us often rely on speed—on making us feel that there is no time to question, no time to organize, no time to rest. The demand to be always available is a demand to be always compliant. When we reclaim our time, we reclaim our power. The refusal to be hurried is, in its own quiet way, a political act. It says: my life is not a resource to be extracted.

Of course, not everyone has the privilege to choose slowness. Many people work multiple jobs, care for children, survive in conditions where time is not their own. I do not want to romanticize poverty or pretend that everyone can simply opt out of the rush. But even within constraints, there are small acts of resistance. A moment of breathing before the next shift. A refusal to check email during a meal. A walk around the block without a destination. These may seem small, but they accumulate. They remind us that we are human beings, not machines.

The Japanese have a term, yutori, which means spaciousness or room to breathe. It was introduced as an educational reform to reduce pressure on students, but the word captures something broader. A life with yutori is one with margins—time for rest, for play, for unexpected encounters. Without margins, any small disruption becomes a crisis. With margins, we can absorb shock and still have energy to care for others.

I think of my grandmother, who never seemed to hurry. She moved slowly through her kitchen, peeling apples with a small knife, humming. As a child, I found this maddening. I wanted to be somewhere, do something. But now I understand that she was not slow because she was incapable of speed. She was slow because she had decided what mattered: the taste of the apples, the warmth of the kitchen, the presence of a grandchild. She was paying attention. She was lingering.

We need more lingerers. More people who will sit on a bench and watch the world. More people who will ask a question and actually wait for the answer. More people who will resist the tyranny of the urgent and choose the important—even when the important is as simple as a conversation, a sunset, a breath. The lost art of lingering is not lost because we forgot how to do it. It is lost because we stopped believing it was worth doing. But it is still there, waiting for us to slow down enough to find it.

In the end, slowness is not about getting less done. It is about doing less in a way that means more. It is about reclaiming the texture of our days, the taste of our food, the sound of our own thoughts. It is about remembering that we are not here merely to be productive. We are here to be present. And presence requires time—not the measured time of clocks and calendars, but the lived time of attention and care. So, today, perhaps try this: walk somewhere without a purpose. Sit for ten minutes without a screen. Let a conversation extend beyond its natural ending. Linger. You might be surprised at what you find.
